paper_title: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to real images.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability for agents is to be able to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the humans camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite impressive advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in principled manner. The acceptability task asks whether particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether tape measure leans. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to the real images. The benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/relantic/realitybench.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: It has been long-term goal to create AI agents that augment human capabilities in the physical world, from early augmented-reality systems for manufacturing and maintenance (Caudell & Mizell, 1992; Feiner et al., 1993; Henderson & Feiner, 2011) to recent egocentric assistants (Wang et al., 2023b; Grauman et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025). These agents can help novice human workers perform tasks that require knowledge, e.g., showing them where to find particular part of machine, or reduce documentation time for expert workers by converting recording of their task performance into structured report. We expect these capabilities to be of increasing interest. Towards this goal, we evaluate performance of current vision language models (VLMs) on two kinds of tasks (Figure 1): acceptability and documentation. Acceptability tasks ask, given natural language specification, whether an image satisfies it, for the purposes of documenting the state of the environment (e.g., to show that work was performed). For example, in solar installation, an installer may request sharp, close-up picture that shows the flashing and lag bolt for every L-foot on solar module mounting rail (glossary: Appendix B). verdict must intersect several conditions at once,

sections.content: Figure 1: The eleven environments of RealityBench with one scorer-acceptable frame from each. Because each scene is rendered in Blender, each frame can be scored programmatically. Under each frame: short form of the environments documentation question and the ground truth. some of them geometric (is the tape seated flush? is the gauge on the module?). Documentation tasks ask, given natural language specification, to extract certain information from the environment that is needed to document the environmentfor example, reading the height of solar module above the roof off of tape measure. Evaluating the capability of agents on these tasks is challenging and expensive. In-field trials give the best ecological validity, but they are resource intensive. Archived in-field data exists in high volume, but suffers from two issues. First, it is restricted in access, limiting reproducibility and transparency. Second, it is imprecisely overseen: single task may generate huge volume of data (e.g., thousands of photos) with human providing only single label for an entire unit (packet), under business pressure, and often assisted by VLMs. The weakness of VLMs at certain visual tasks makes VLM-based processing of archived field data problematic. This creates mechanistic uncertaintyit is unclear what VLM should be able to conclude from each image. We therefore take simulation approach. RealityBench renders eleven environments in Blender (Figure 1), each with an associated acceptability and documentation task, from rooftop solar installation (seven) and vehicle repair (four). This overcomes both issueswe release the rendered benchmark publicly under permissive license and task success is programmatically evaluable using the environment state. This programmatic evaluation is challenging in the same way alignment to human preferences ishumans may have different views on how the natural language specification should be translated into requirements. Nonetheless, on held-out frames the scorer agrees with the majority of our human raters on 82% of frames, close to the 7692% at which an individual rater agrees with the others (Section 4). We evaluate 26 models on benchmark of 1,378 frames from our simulator. While simulation-based benchmarking has impressive flexibility, it is often difficult to know whether the results translate to the real world. We are able to estimate this gap through evaluations on in-field images procured from real-world physical work tasks, and real world reenactments (for one measuring task, which we release publicly). Model rankings transfer on all three matched documentation questions: across 22 models, Spearman ρ 0.63 per question at 0.002. This is evidence that the simulated tasks predict which models do well on real photographs. Our results provide insights into both what VLMs can perceive and how they judge. Documentation scores are high when the answer is text in frame (labels, plates, directory cards), except for long or unusual strings, and low on measurement (reading tape at the crossing) and on judgments about small parts or relations (whether tape leans, whether lag bolt is present). On acceptability, the best models score about as well as single non-author rater (F1 0.61 against 0.59). We trace acceptability

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Assistants and datasets for physical work. Large egocentric corpora have the model observe the worker. Ego4D and Ego-Exo4D (Grauman et al., 2022; 2024) and procedural datasets such as Assembly101, IndustReal and CaptainCook4D (Sener et al., 2022; Schoonbeek et al., 2024; Peddi et al., 2024) label steps, mistakes (Lee et al., 2024) and proficiency. HoloAssist (Wang et al., 2023b) records remote instructor guiding worker in real time, and portable egocentric VLM assistants are beginning to appear (Huang et al., 2025). For inspections, VLMs have been evaluated as constructionsafety inspectors (Chen & Zou, 2025) and as unified industrial-inspection models, where they proved brittle against task-specific baselines (Wallace et al., 2025). These datasets are video-centric and label the workthey dont ask whether captured view is adequate proof that the work was done. We found no public dataset of worker-submitted proof-of-work photos judged for acceptability. Synthetic environments and sim-to-real. Rendered data with exact ground truth has long history as training data (Richter et al., 2016; Roberts et al., 2021) and as diagnostic test bed, e.g., CLEVR (Johnson et al., 2017) and Super-CLEVR (Li et al., 2023), which varies scene factors independently. Generators include Kubric, BlenderProc and Infinigen (Greff et al., 2022; Denninger et al., 2023; Raistrick et al., 2023), and embodied simulators include ProcTHOR and Habitat (Deitke et al., 2022; Savva et al., 2019). Domain randomization (Tobin et al., 2017) and synthetic spatial training that improves real-image benchmarks (Ray et al., 2025) show that variation can improve sim-to-real transfer. We know of no prior work that measures whether VLM rankings on rendered benchmark match rankings on real photos of the same task. Judging image quality. No-reference image quality assessment scores perceptual quality from statistics (Mittal et al., 2012; 2013) or learned models (Ke et al., 2021), and recent work puts the question to VLMs directly: CLIP-IQA (Wang et al., 2023a) with antonym prompts, Q-Bench (Wu et al., 2024a) as low-level-vision benchmark, and Q-Align and DepictQA (Wu et al., 2024b; You et al., 2024) for calibrated scores and language explanations. These judge quality independent of content. Task-defined acceptability appears in mobile document capture, where frame is good if downstream OCR succeeds (Burie et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018; Bulatov et al., 2020), and in insurance imaging, where customer photos feed damage estimation (Mallios et al., 2023) and VLMs are benchmarked on claims imagery (Lin et al., 2025), but there the photos are assumed adequate. Scoring an image against specification. TIFA and Davidsonian Scene Graph (Hu et al., 2023; Cho et al., 2024) decompose prompt into questions answered by VQA model, VQAScore (Lin

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: et al., 2024) asks single yes/no, and GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023) runs hand-written detector pipeline over object state, reporting agreement with annotators close to inter-annotator agreement. Visual programming (Gupta & Kembhavi, 2023; Surís et al., 2023; Cho et al., 2023) and LLMwritten reward code over simulator state (Ma et al., 2024) generate the verifier itself. Our scorers are hand-written programs over privileged scene state, closest in spirit to GenEval, and we validate them against human ratings as that literature does. We do not use VLM as the reference scorer, partly because studies of multimodal LLMs as judges find absolute scoring inconsistent even for frontier models (Chen et al., 2024b). Fine-grained perception in VLMs. BLINK (Fu et al., 2024b) finds frontier models near chance on tasks humans solve at glance, MMVP (Tong et al., 2024) traces failures on orientation, counting and small details to the CLIP encoder, and HallusionBench (Guan et al., 2024) separates answering from priors from misreading the image. Spatial benchmarks report that metric questions are among the hardest (Yang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024a), and PhysBench (Chow et al., 2025) covers physical properties and relations broadly. Reading text is well studied, e.g., through scene-text and document VQA (Singh et al., 2019; Mathew et al., 2021) and OCRBench (Liu et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024a), which singles out non-semantic strings such as serial numbers as weakness. Closest to our tape and gauge tasks, MeasureBench (Lin et al., 2026) benchmarks reading values off instruments in real and synthesized images and finds that frontier VLMs struggle, while specialist readers trained on synthetic gauges remain competitive (Leon-Alcazar et al., 2024; Mueez et al., 2026).

sections.title: 3 ENVIRONMENTS
sections.content: We construct 11 environments in Blender 4.5.12 in two settings: rooftop solar installation (seven) and vehicle repair (four). Each environment uses shared model of the phone camera: phone is drawn per scene (main lens 2428 mm full-frame equivalent, sensor width 5.69.8 mm, f/1.62.4, and on some phones ultra-wide and telephoto lenses and digital zoom), each frame is rendered in landscape or portrait at that phones effective focal length, and the aperture is set from the physical lens so that Cycles renders phones depth of field. 70% of frames are focused on the target with steady hand, 15% have the autofocus locked elsewhere and 15% have hand shake over shutter time drawn log-uniformly from 1/500 to 1/25 s. Sensor noise, white balance, tone mapping, chromatic aberration, vignetting and JPEG re-encode are applied after the render. Each environment has an acceptability and documentation task. The acceptability tasks ask whether photo satisfies natural language condition. The documentation tasks ask the model to write some property of the environment to structured JSON format. Example prompts are in Appendix C. Why these tasks? First, they are derived from tasks where VLMs fell short on real field images. Second, they test models along many axes. For example, rail_attachment asks whether close-up shows the flashing and lag bolt of single roof attachment, testing recognition of small hardware in clutter. Other tasks ask the model to read text and capture an image that shows that text clearly to human. Finally, while there is body of VLM work in structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance, and not rigorously studied. Together, these tasks allow us to assess perception and understanding in nuanced way.

sections.title: 3.1 ROOFTOP SOLAR INSTALLATION
sections.content: Six of the seven solar environments are on the tilted roof of house where solar array is being or has been installed. Five share one procedural roof scene: the roof rectangle and pitch, the shingle courses, the house body under the roof (lap siding or brick), gable or shed roof, chimney (about half of the scenes), ladder leaning on the eave, the array layout and the sun are all drawn per scene from the generators distributions. The background is sky-only HDRI panorama with the sun lamp aligned to the panoramas own sun. horizon_peak uses one of 21 CC0 house meshes instead, re-covered with the same procedural shingle courses and trims, placed inside full 360 panorama. The seventh, breaker_label, is set at the houses load center on wall. We follow an installation in order. The arrays rails are held to the roof by L-feet, each lag-bolted into rafter through sheet of flashing slipped under the shingles which, together, anchor the rail

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: and prevent leakage. rail_attachment asks for close-up of one attachment that shows the L-foot, its flashing and the lag bolt, and asks whether the bolt and the flashing are present. Under the modules, the wire should not touch the shingles: wire_adequacy asks for photograph of the wires lowest point, and asks whether any wire touches the roof (the requirement also mentions hard bends, which the scorer does not check separately). The module must stand clear of the roof: tape_gap asks for tape measure standing up to the module frame, and asks for the number at the crossing, the true perpendicular gap and whether the tape leans. The modules slope is recorded with digital angle gauge: slope_gauge asks for the gauge sitting on the module, aligned with the slope, with the module visible (the scorer also requires some of the modules edge in view, since alignment cannot be judged without it), and asks for the reading. Each piece of equipment is photographed by its nameplate: equipment_label asks for legible nameplate and for its brand, model and serial number and what it is on. From the ridge, the installer photographs the skyline in every direction, which records the obstructions that shade the array. horizon_peak asks for photo, taken from the peak, of the skyline in one direction with little of the houses own roof along the bottom, and asks whether the horizon is visible and level. Finally, the array ties into the houses electrical panel: breaker_label asks for square-on, legible close-up of the circuit directory card and for its full contents, the main breaker amperage and every circuits name and amperage.

sections.title: 3.2 VEHICLE REPAIR
sections.content: The photographer is in parking lot with multiple vehicles from set of nine meshes, with the subject car identified by color and body style (the silver sedan). damaged vehicle arriving at repair shop is first documented as whole. car_view asks for particular face of the car (front, rear, driver or passenger side) straight on, with the whole car in frame from about two car lengths, and asks which face is shown and the body style. The damage is then photographed up close: in damage_view, procedurally generated dent, scratch or rust mark on panel must be photographed square-on from about an arms length, with part of the adjacent panel in frame for context, and the model is asked the kind of damage and its severity (minor, moderate or severe, by surface area). The vehicles identity is recorded: car_plate asks for the mounted license plate close up and legible, and for its characters and the state named on it. Finally the shop issues repair order, written with the vehicles VIN on hand-held board and photographed with the car so the two are tied together: ro_board asks for the board, legible, with the car in the same frame, and for the RO number and the VIN.

sections.title: 4 BUILDING THE BENCHMARK SET AND ACCEPTABILITY SCORER
sections.content: For each of the 11 scenes, we render 100 frames with the camera drawn from that environments pose distribution. We perform additional positive sampling for the seven environments where random frames are rarely acceptable, for total of 1,450 initial frames. In ro_board, 29 frames were withdrawn because of defect in the board texture, leaving 1,421 frames. We define an acceptability scorer for each environment, which is an intersection of acceptability terms. Some acceptability terms are computed directly from the scene after the camera is placed, including in-frame and occlusion by ray casting, distances, view angles, and pixels per unit length. Another set of terms is read off the rendered frame itself, including sharpness at the target, the texts contrast against its paper and its blown-out fraction, the wires pixel count and edge contrast, and the labels paper luminance. Acceptability is orthogonal to work completenessunacceptable work can be acceptably documented. Documentation answers are scored against the scenes ground truth. Details are in Tables 1 and 2. We call frames that pass the acceptability scorer scorer-acceptable. We tune the scorer to simulate human judgment. Six raters (four authors and two colleagues) judged 30 random frames per environment for acceptability, against the requirement text the models see and without seeing the scorers verdict: two raters judged all of them, three judged 2025 per environment, and one author judged only tape_gap and damage_view (4.05.1 ratings per frame, Table 13).1 We split this set once, by frame, into 60% used to adjust the scorer and set the gray zones (described below) and 40% looked at once, after the scorer was frozen. On each held-out frame with at least three ratings we take the raters majority as the reference (95 frames after excluding ties). The tuned 1Ten of the rated ro_board frames were among those later withdrawn; their ratings are kept in the scorer tuning and in the agreement figures below.

It errs on the strict side: it accepts 4 of the 62 frames the majority rejects and rejects 13 of the 33 that the majority accepts. An individual rater agrees with the majority of the other raters on 7692% (67% for the author who rated two environments, on 18 frames, Table 13). We opted to drop the acceptability task for car_plate, where human raters disagreed on small but legible plates, and the acceptability task for frames of rail_attachment that clearly show an attachment with its lag bolt or flashing missing, due to task ambiguity. We removed the scorer requirement that the horizon_peak horizon be level, which the requirement text did not ask for. After these reductions and the gray zones below, 1,378 frames remained. Of these, 1,265 are scored for acceptability, and the 547 scorer-acceptable frames (including those of car_plate) are scored for documentation.2 Acceptability gray zones. Natural language descriptions that are used in the field are ambiguous (what does arms length mean?). We want to avoid marking down models that reasonably interpret natural language. Where the wording leaves range open, or our human raters disagree with each other over it, we mark that range of the term as gray (four zones in Table 1). For example, in damage_view, which asks for photo from about arms length, camera distances between 1.5 and 3 are gray. frame whose verdict depends only on gray term is not scored for any model. We drop 43 frames from the acceptability set this way. Other metrics. We report the cost of the whole set at the developers own list API price  (Table 7)  , with thinking tokens priced at the output rate.3 We served three models ourselves (Gemma 4 E4B, LFM2.5-VL-3B, Qwen3.5-4B), which we do not attempt to price due to differences between selfhosting and API costs. We report the mean number of thinking tokens per item (where provider reports only an output count, the count minus the tokens of the reply we received) and the fraction of answers that match the stated grammar.

sections.title: 5 REAL-WORLD DATA
sections.content: For three of the tasks we have approximate real-world equivalents, which let us estimate the sim-toreal gap. Reading tape measures. We find that reading the measured distance off tape measure precisely is one of the most challenging synthetic tasks. To test whether this result transfers, we photographed tape measure held against everyday objects (monitors, laptop, benches, tables, fence, whiteboard, car battery) and recorded the ground truth for each measurand with caliper or careful human tape read: 133 readings on 84 photos of 35 items across 12 scenes, which we release. Each reading is asked with prompt of the same form as tape_gaps, naming the object and the measurement in place of the module and the gap, and scored as read within 1/8 in of the ground truth. Assessing car damage. We use photographs of damaged vehicles from the real world. For car_views face question, one author labeled 117 real frames with every side and third of the car they showthe models answer was marked correct if it names one of them. This is similar to car_views documentation task. For damage_views severity question, one author rated the 63 photos of damaged panels on the documentation tasks severity scale.

sections.title: 6.1 RESULTS
sections.content: On synthetic data, models spread widely on both tracks (acceptability F1 0.390.61, documentation 0.620.84), with the two rankings in approximate agreement (Spearman ρ = 0.69, < 0.001). On each track, we call the leader and the models whose paired 95% interval against it includes zero the top group  (Table 6)  . On acceptability, GPT-6 Astra leads (0.61, $30.05), with Claude Opus 5.5 (0.58, $16.36), GLM-5.3 Flash (0.57, $1.30) and Gemini 3.5 Flash (0.56, $7.36) in the top group. On documentation, Gemini 3.8 Flash leads (0.84, $7.16), with Claude Opus 5.5 (0.83, $16.36), GPT-6 Astra (0.83, $30.05), Claude Fable 5.1 (0.83, $41.35) and Qwen 3.8 Max (0.82, $38.19) in the top group. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 are the only models in both top groups. The best open-weight model on acceptability is GLM-5.3 Flash, and on documentation the much smaller Gemma 4 31B (0.79, $0.70). Routing across models helps documentation but not acceptability:

The majority of all models reaches F1 0.60 and documentation 0.83 at $322on par with or worse than the best single model. On the cost axis, the models fall into three separated groups: those costing over $4 for the set ($4.80 41.35), six costing under $2 ($0.691.30, which we call moderately priced), and the unpriced models we served ourselves. The moderately priced group contains three open-weight models (Gemma 4 31B, Gemma 4 26B-A4B and GLM-5.3 Flash) and three closed-weight models (GPT-6 Luna, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite and GPT-5.6 Luna). The top group on acceptability within the moderately priced band is GLM-5.3 Flash (0.57, $1.30) and GPT-5.6 Luna (0.53, $1.18), and on documentation, Gemma 4 31B (0.79, $0.70) alone. Two of these three top group models are open-weight and thus make especially attractive targets for fine-tuning. The unpriced band is on par with the lowest scoring priced models on both tracks, with LFM2.5VL-3B and Gemma 4 E4B at the top of it (F1 0.43 and 0.42, documentation 0.68 and 0.69). These models are exciting because they can run on-device, with low latency and no network dependence. Real-world images. Figure 2 (bottom) and Table 14 give, per model, the synthetic and real scores on the three matched questions. We see the tasks have broadly consistent difficulties between real and synthetic environments, with tape reading hardest on both, followed by damage severity, followed by naming the seen face of the car (which is saturated for top models). The rankings transfer, with Spearman ρ of 0.630.79 (p 0.002) with the worst transfer on damage severity.4 Human raters. Using only the raters who were not involved in designing the scorer, single rater scores an F1 of 0.59 (95% CI 0.500.67) against the scorer. Individual raters are noisythe scorer tracks their majority. We cannot distinguish the strongest models from single human rater on acceptability. We perform an approximate cost comparison. Our raters took 812 per frame (including the documentation fields) while doing other work; they are not expert raters and did not know they were being timed, so we allow for faster work. At 312 per item and $10/h (a somewhat arbitrary lower bound) to $35.91/h (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2026), one human pass over the 1,378 items costs roughly $11165, against $16.36 for Claude Opus 5.5 and $30.05 for GPT-6 Astra. Across generations, models improve on score and cost at once, so if the trend holds they will overtake single rater on these tasks. Their remaining weaknesses are specific, and we turn to them next.

sections.title: 7 ANALYSIS
sections.content: What is easy and hard for models? Figure 3 divides the 24 documentation fields into three groups: reading (transcribe text or digits), judgment (a categorical scene state) and measurement (for reading tape measures) (details: Table 10). Models are very strong at reading: eight of the ten reading fields score 0.901.00 averaged over models. Long or unusual strings are still hard on average: the 17-character VIN (mean 0.59) and the gauges seven-segment display (0.66), though Gemini 3.8 Flash scores 0.89 and 0.95. On judgment fields, those whose answer fills the frame are easy: what the label is on (mean 0.95), whether the horizon is visible (0.98) or level (0.91), the kind of damage (0.89), the cars face (0.83) and body style (0.81). The hard ones concern small part or relation: whether the lag bolt is present (0.67, best 0.82), how severe the damage is (0.61, best 0.75), whether the wire touches the roof (0.57, best 0.74) and whether the tape is leaning (0.55, best 0.82). Reading tape measure is the hardest tested task: the number at the crossing is within 1/8 in 11% of the time on average (best 36%, Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol), and the true gap within 1/4 in 23% (best 48%, Opus 5.5); as we saw, this difficulty carries over to real photographs. Across models, reading score is not detectably correlated with judgment (Spearman ρ = 0.23, = 0.27), while judgment and measurement are strongly correlated (ρ = 0.61). sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced RealityBench, eleven rendered environments from rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair. The environments are simulators, not image sets, so they extend to new tasks and to closedloop guidance. Each environment poses two tasks field agent needs, both scored programmatically from the scene: judging whether photograph is adequate proof of work and reading the task-relevant

Acceptability, however, is harder to pin down, since raters disagree with each other, and the best models are level with single non-author rater. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene. Rankings on rendered frames transfer to real photographs on all three matched documentation questions.

sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools for the following tasks with required disclosure: proposing or refining hypotheses; designing or providing feedback on research methodology or experiments; implementing methods; cleaning and reformatting data; and interpreting results. sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Human ratings. The acceptability ratings used to validate the scorers and to compare models against people were produced by four of the authors and two colleagues, rating rendered frames of inanimate scenes; one author also labeled the vehicle photographs of Section 5 with the face shown and the damage severity. No personal data was collected from the raters, so no ethics review was sought. Real photographs. The tape-measure photographs were taken by an author of their own objects; we release them. The vehicle damage photographs are used with permission. We use them only to score model answers, do not release them, do not reproduce them in the paper, and sent them only to providers whose data-retention terms met ours. Conflicts of interest. The benchmark measures the general capability of third-party models rather than any product produced by the authors, and the API models were run through their public APIs at list prices and the three open-weight models on rented GPUs. Assets and licenses. Every third-party 3D asset in the environments is CC0 or CC-BY and is listed with its license and attribution in the released datasets attribution file. Potential harms. system that judges photographs of completed work could be used to pressure workers or to automate rejection of legitimate work. We argue that better evaluation of model capabilities is important for making societal decisions about the use of AI in human work.

sections.title: A LIMITATIONS
sections.content: We evaluate single frames, whereas workers would naturally produce video. The scorer is one reading of each requirement, validated against six raters on 30 frames per environment, and it errs on the strict side. The human comparison uses non-expert raters, and its cost is rough range. The error tracing covers wrong rejections in the three environments where acceptability and documentation share field. The real-world comparison covers three documentation questions and no acceptability task. The eleven environments come from two kinds of work. We test general-purpose models zero-shot at provider defaults, not specialist readers or detectors, and model versions and prices change quickly.

sections.content: Table 14: Synthetic against real, per model, three matched questions. Synthetic: the share of scoreracceptable synthetic frames whose field is right (tape_gap reading within 1/8 in; car_view face; damage_view severity on the frames where the scorer finds the damage readable: sharp, visible and resolved, framing not required). Real: our tape photos read within 1/8 in (133 readings on 84 photos of 35 items); the face named is one the labels list as visible (117 side-determinable frames); severity on the 59 real damaged-panel photos an author rated on the prompts area scale after the model runs, blind to the models answers (4 rated cant tell are left out). Brackets: 95% bootstrap intervals over frames, or over items for the tape photos. Across the 22 models, synthetic against real (Spearman, Pearson): tape ρ = 0.68 (p = 0.001), = 0.82 (p < 0.001); face ρ = 0.79 (p < 0.001), = 0.85 (p < 0.001); severity ρ = 0.63 (p = 0.002), = 0.58 (p = 0.005). Not run on the real photos: Qwen 3.8 Max, Muse Spark 1.3, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Tape replies cut by the output cap, left out: GLM-5.3 Flash 54, Qwen 3.8 27B 15, Qwen 3.5 397B-A17B 8.
